articles.title: Mega Pixel 11 series leak leaves nothing to the imagination
articles.content: TL;DR A new leak has given away all the specs and pricing details of the upcoming Pixel 11 series. The phones are said to feature the Tensor G6 processor, Titan M3 co-processor, up to 16GB of RAM, and up to 1TB of storage. The Pixel 11 is expected to start at $899, the Pixel 11 Pro at $1,099, the Pixel 11 Pro XL at $1,299, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold at $1,899. As we approach Google’s August 12 event, we’re seeing a slew of leaks for the upcoming Pixel 11 series and even the Pixel Watch 5 . Now, a new leak has revealed detailed specs and pricing of all the upcoming Pixel phones. Pixel 11 specs and price According to Android Headlines , the Pixel 11 will come with a 6.3-inch OLED display with a resolution of 2,424 x 1,080 pixels, 3,000 nits of brightness, and a 60-120Hz adaptive refresh rate.

articles.title: 5 best new Netflix movies and shows to stream this week (August 3-9)
articles.content: If you're looking to find what new movies and shows Netflix is adding this week, I've got you covered. The streaming service is adding 23 new movies and shows this week. But there are quite a few titles still worth adding to your watchlist. Top of the list is " The Last House " season 2 . This new sci-fi thriller flick stars Greta Lee and Wagner Moura in a fight for survival. I can't wait to see it. If thrillers aren't your thing, though, you might prefer " My Life with the Walter Boys " season 3 . This drama series may be centered around teens, but messy relationships and near-death experiences are for all ages. There are some other options if those headliners don't speak to you. " Let's Marry Harry " tries to succeed where "Too Hot to Handle" and "Perfect Match" failed and find a partner for Netflix reality star Harry Jowsey. Meanwhile, " Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy " is a new documentary that will have you ready to never eat a chicken sandwich again. Finally, for those who don't mind subtitles, " Death Inc. " season 4 marks the end of a beloved Spanish comedy series with a twisted sense of humor. Those aren't the only movies, shows and live events to add to your watchlist this week, though. Here's the full schedule of everything new on Netflix over the next seven days, along with my top picks for what you need to stream. Don't forget to check out everything new on Netflix in August 2026 for even more movies and shows to check out. New on Netflix this week: Top picks 'The Last House' Genre: Sci-fi thriller movie What it's about: "The Last House" centers around a family of four. Led by mom Riley (Greta Lee) and dad Jason (Wagner Moura), they suddenly find themselves trapped in their house. But as the days turn to weeks, they realize the whole world was trapped, and they're now the only ones left. Why you should watch it: I'd be game to watch anything with Lee and Moura in it. But this movie looks seriously creepy. So I'm even more sold than I already was. Watch "The Last House" on Netflix starting August 7 'My Life with the Walter Boys' season 3 Genre: Teen drama series What's it about? "My Life with the Walter Boys" stars Nikki Rodriguez as Jackie Howard. She's been orphaned, so she leaves Manhattan and starts over in Colorado with the Walters. But as if the culture shock wasn't bad enough, the Walters have seven boys, and they come with plenty of drama. Why you need to watch it: If you thought this show would manage to avoid "Game of Thrones" comparisons, I have bad news. In season 2, Nikki, who had been dating Alex Walter (Ashby Gentry), declared her feelings for Cole, another Walter brother. But if you can get past the Targaryen-esque love triangle, people do seem to love this coming-of-age drama. Watch "My Life with the Walter Boys" season 3 on Netflix starting August 6 'Let's Marry Harry' Genre: Reality dating series What it's about: Harry Jowsey was a breakout star in multiple Netflix reality shows. There's just one problem. He could never find love. In this new series, Netflix aims to fix that. By the end of eight episodes, hopefully one of the 20 women competing for his heart will have said yes, but it'd be incredible television if they didn't. Why you should watch it: "Too Hot to Handle" and "Perfect Match" were unable to find Harry the one. What's that they say about insanity? Something about doing the same thing and expecting different results? Hopefully, "Let's Marry Harry" holds to a different saying: third time's the charm. Watch the first seven episodes of "Let's Marry Harry" on Netflix starting August 5 'Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy' Genre: Documentary movie What it's about: Stand-up comedian Mo Gilligan is ditching the hour-long special. Instead, he's doing a 28-day experiment to determine how bad it would be to eat fast food fried chicken every day for a month. He might get more than just a few unwelcome pounds. Why you should watch it: Look, we already did "Supersize Me." So if you liked…
articles.author: Malcolm McMillan

articles.title: IT boss left root session open for bring-your-kid-to-work day
articles.content: WHO, ME? Comedian W.C. Fields is credited with the aphorism "Never work with children or animals," which The Register mentions because half of it has some relevance to this week's edition of "Who, Me?" – the reader-contributed column chronicling the ups and downs of working in tech. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Stockley" who shared a horror story that took place in the 1990s. At the time, Stockley worked for a company that ran an IBM RS/6000, one of Big Blue's brood of Unix machines. "The business was run on BASIC, with code going back 25 years," Stockley wrote. When much of that software was written, memory was measured in kilobytes. "Programs had to be broken into chunks, which were called sequentially with the CHAIN command," he told Who, Me? The company's tech may have been a bit crusty, but it made up for that by being a lovely family-friendly workplace – so much so that it invited staff to bring their kids in for Halloween trick-or-treating. Stockley told us that one Halloween, the company's IT boss knew the children would disrupt work, so started the day's data processing early, setting the chained programs in motion. Then his wife and children arrived ahead of the Halloween festivities. The boss therefore parked his children in his office, in front of terminals connected to the RS/6000. The terminals were switched on and logged in as root. In Stockley's telling, the boss's nine-year-old daughter had recently seen a movie in which a young girl somehow acquired Unix skills and saved the day by typing "SHUTDOWN." And when the boss returned to his office, his daughter greeted him by saying: "Look, Daddy! SHUTDOWN worked just like it did in the movie!" Stockley recalls that the boss needed 36 hours to repair the damage his daughter had caused. Have kids messed with your tech? If so, don't mess about! Click here to send your story to Who, Me? so we can prove the point about working with kids on a future Monday. ®

articles.title: Samsung might kill one of the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s rear cameras
articles.content: Credit: Brady Snyder / Android Authority TL;DR The Galaxy S27 Ultra will reportedly drop the 3x camera and switch to a triple rear camera system. This comes after years of Samsung’s Ultra phones offering a quad camera setup. This 3x camera is effectively obsolete, but it’s still handy for portraits and macro photography. Samsung’s Galaxy S Ultra phones have offered four rear cameras since 2021’s Galaxy S21 Ultra, with the Galaxy S26 Ultra also following this trend. Unfortunately, two sources have now claimed that Samsung could drop one camera next year. Veteran tipster Ice Universe refuted an X user’s post claiming that the Galaxy S27 Ultra will have a second rear telephoto camera. Instead, the leaker says the upcoming phone only has a 50MP 5x telephoto shooter.
articles.author: Hadlee Simons

articles.title: These iClever Q950s might be the best kid headphones I’ve ever tried
articles.content: Headphones that are specifically labeled for children tend to feature a ton of drawbacks, especially when it comes to sound quality. That said, why we recommend specific kid headphones is because most of the ones we test feature volume limiters designed to protect little ears from future hearing damage or loss. With that in mind, the iClever Q950 might be the best kid headphones I’ve ever tested. They’re comfortable and sound amazing for kids’ cans. No, they won’t replace the best headphones for adults, but a kid won’t complain, and even most grown-ups will enjoy listening to this set. Read my full iClever Q950 review to find out why. iClever Q950 review: Specs iClever Q950 Specs Price $69 Headphone style Over ear Drivers 40mm Frequency response 20Hz - 20kHz Safe volume limited 80dBA Battery capacity 500mAh Durability No IP rating Connectivity Wired, 3.5mm cable or Bluetooth v6.0, USB-C charging port Weight 9.9 oz (238 grams) Colors Blue/Purple iClever Q950 review: Price & availability The iClever Q950 cost $69 at Amazon , but we’ve seen them a bit lower at $59 during sales events. Even at full price, these are pretty good value for money. The Q950 competes with other iClever offerings like its colorful Auraa headphones ($39) and the Puro Sound Lab BT2200s ($99) or the extremely low-cost $20 JBL Junior 320s . I don’t think you’d go wrong with the other options, especially if you’re trying to save a buck, but personally, I’d recommend the Q950 as the middle ground. Plus, they sound better than the other offerings. iClever Q950 review: Design (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Compared to most kid headphones, the iClever Q950 look more sophisticated while also clearly being made for children. Compared to the usual grays, blacks and whites that make up adult headphones, the Q950 are quite colorful but not quite as garish as they could be. Largely that has to do with the bright blue or purple hues. The holders have a pleasant metallic sheen. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Outside of colors, these are pretty durable headphones; I performed a couple of drop tests and twisted the headphones around a few times and never felt afraid that I was about to break them, though I’m sure an enterprising tot could destroy them. They’re over-ear headphones with extendable ears that fold in, but can also turn out to lay flat if you want. They won’t disappear, but it gives you some flexibility, especially when trying to store them in a backpack. For extra protection, the Q950 does come with a bulky carry case that can hold charging wires and the 3.5mm wire. The case isn’t as bag-friendly, but you can stuff some Pokémon cards in there if you want. Comfort (Image credit: Tom's Guide) With comfort in mind, one of my personal bugaboos with over-ear headphones is the headband. If I notice the band during a listening session, it becomes grating. I never noticed it with the Q950, which is one of the highest compliments I can pay. Despite my adult ears, the ear cups didn’t squish them, and they fully cover a kid's ears, meaning there isn’t sound leakage. I was able to wear the iClever headphones for a full workday without noticing them. At 9.9 ounces (238 grams), these are some of the heaviest kid headphones I’ve tested. As an adult, I didn’t find the weight uncomfortable, but while 8 or 9 ounces isn’t much for grown-ups, it does add up for your kid. My son tried the headphones, and he didn’t find them uncomfortable, but he has complimented lighter headphones like the JBL Junior 320 when we’ve had them before. In comparison, those headphones only weigh 4 ounces, less than half the weight of the Q950. Connectivity (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The iClever Q950 comes with both wired and Bluetooth connectivity. I’m a big proponent of 3.5mm wired connections when they’re available. These headphones come with a 3.5mm wire that sends the audio pretty cleanly. I can’t tell how they’ll hold up in the long run but for now it seems pretty sturdy. Q950 features Bluetooth…

articles.title: We asked over 3,000 people what their biggest lawn care challenges were — and one answer came out on top
articles.content: Summer is the best time to get out into your garden and enjoy your outside space. It's also one of the hardest times to keep your lawn in top condition, battling with hot weather, dry soil, and all of that extra use. While I've been using 3 drought-proofing steps to protect my lawn during heatwaves , I can't help but notice I'm still struggling with specific issues. And I know I'm not the only one. So, it only felt right to put it to our readers and ask: "What is the biggest problem you have with your lawn?" Over 3,000 of you answered, and here's what came out on top. Even better, I've got tips on how to fix it. The number one lawn problem, according to readers (Image credit: Shutterstock) There was one resounding answer that came from our poll, far outweighing other issues, and that's bare patches. With a massive 3,079 votes totalling 64% of our readers' answers, it's a patchy lawn that seems to be causing the most bother. To give you an idea of just how dominant this issue is, the second issue was crabgrass that received 625 votes (13%) followed by dog wee stains at 451 votes (9%) and dandelions at 388 votes (8%). And I completely agree, struggling with bare patches myself and trying desperately to make sure my grass looks even across my lawn. Fortunately, there's plenty of solutions to try that we've covered across a range of how-to guides. I'll delve into some of the top tips below and hopefully next time we run a poll, bare patches won't be such a problem. How to tackle bare patches From 5-minute quick fixes to step-by-step guides , depending on how much time you've got on your hands, these are the top tips I recommend to try out on that patchy lawn. 1. Try overseeding (Image credit: Shutterstock) It might seem like all hope is lost when your grass suddenly turns into a bare, soil patch on your lawn, but you can reapply seed to help with regrowth. It's called overseeding and it's a method used to block out weeds, cover up bare turf, and ultimately create a lawn that is covered with even grass. But, you may find that even when you've overseeded it, you're still experiencing patchiness. There's a few reasons for that, but nothing our next step can't try and solve. Covering up to 85 sq. ft. Scott's EZ Seed is specifically-designed for fixing bare patches on your lawn. For best results, apply it when the temperatures sitting between 60°F and 80°F. All you have to do is prep the area, evenly apply the seed and water it until no more water is being absorbed. View Deal 2. Reseed if the first go didn't take (Image credit: Shutterstock) Sometimes one overseeding session isn't quite enough and that's a problem answered by Chrissie Handley, lawn care specialist at Online Turf when we spoke with her about yellow patches on lawns: "You tend to lose some seed either from the birds picking some off the ground, or through wind blowing it away, or heavy rain can also wash some away, giving you a sparse regrowth." The answer for this? Reseed and focus on even distribution across your lawn, in case the way you're applying it by hand is too thinly spread. 3. Add a layer of topsoil (Image credit: Shutterstock) Additionally, to protect the seed, you can add a thin layer of topsoil afterwards. As Handley recommends: "This can help stop the birds from picking it off, and also helps the seed make good contact with the ground, improving your germination rate." Consider it an extra layer of protection, prompting grass growth and hopefully leading to a less patchy lawn. 4. Try a good fertilizer (Image credit: Shutterstock) Finally, you might want to think about adding some fertilizer to your lawn. Sure, it's hard to know how often you should fertilize your lawn and when to do it , but as advice widely varies it's always a good idea to check the type of fertilizer you're using and what job you want it to do. If you can nail down some good practice with fertilizer, as well as choosing one that's suitable for the job, you can tackle those patchy areas…

articles.title: Hollywood Fights AI In Public While Quietly Building It Into Movies
articles.content: Even as Hollywood performers protest and Hollywood studios sue "in their war on AI," reports the Los Angeles Times, "the entertainment industry is deepening its dependence on it." Among hundreds of job postings in late June, more than one in 10 was likely connected to AI. The top studios' public postings suggest they have been recruiting people to build AI tools. They are also recruiting teams to defend their intellectual property against unauthorized AI use. "There are plenty of studios that are hiring [for AI] but never talk about it in public," said Yoland Yan, a co-founder of ComfyUI, a company that helps studios juggle different AI tools. Companies have been hesitant to detail how they use generative AI in film production — partly because they are concerned about consumer and union backlash. Some in Hollywood described AI use as the new cosmetic surgery, where everyone knows it is happening, but few will admit to it... Although some companies may be shy about sharing their AI plans, big stars who don't have to answer to others have been more open about their embrace of the new technology for storytelling. Rejecting AI is like picking a horse and buggy over a car, said "Star Wars" creator George Lucas. "Artificial intelligence means it's much easier for us to make movies," he told a trade magazine earlier this year. "There's nothing you can do about it. That's progress. It's the future." Some in Hollywood have a softer stance on artificial intelligence, with studios cutting deals with AI companies, and filmmakers like Martin Scorsese backing AI companies. Ben Affleck launched an AI film tech company then sold it to Netflix for half a billion dollars. When launching InterPositive, Affleck said he wanted to keep "storytelling human" by building AI tools that could fix lighting, generate missing shots and other things while "keeping creative decisions in the hands of artists...." Disney, Netflix and Amazon had job postings that were about using AI on the creative side of the business. Universal, Paramount, Warner Bros. and Sony had job ads suggesting they were also using AI but for marketing, distribution and audience analytics. The postings suggest the Disney, Netflix and Amazon studios are building repeatable AI workflows for visual effects, animation, sound and dubbing. The companies also seem to be building in-house teams to develop custom generative-AI models, while also using third-party software. None of the jobs advertised were to create AI that wrote scripts or created AI actors. Ironically, the Times used Claude Code to build a scraper to identify the job postings, their article acknowledges. Three Disney jobs were for "content security," assessing AI tools and guarding against piracy, watermarking and rights-protection work. But Disney is also hiring PhD-level talent "to study 'computer graphics and AI' for Pixar and Disney films," according to the article, and "people to 'bridge the gap between research and practical studio application.'" Disney-owned visual effects shops Industrial Light & Magic "was searching for supervisors to 'explore emerging technologies (including AI/Machine Learning)' to develop new production workflows." Audio post-production unit Skywalker Sound "seemed to be recruiting to build proprietary AI models for soundtracks, voice separation, and voice transfer, the process of taking a speaker's tone and pitch, and applying it to new content." Amazon "was hiring a principal AI executive to drive AI-tool adoption across production, plus roles in operations automation and LLM content classification." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: A personal trainer says this is the 10-minute mobility routine everyone should do to improve walking strength
articles.content: Building strength and range of motion in your body will keep your muscles, joints and ligaments prepared for walks, walking workouts, or other forms of sports and exercises you enjoy. While building strong bones and muscles is your greatest anti-aging tool, mobility is also the hidden secret to longevity; combining both is the weapon you need. When considering stretching versus mobility for your body, you'll need to decide what it is you want to gain. While stretching may offer you benefits in flexibility, mobility routines will help you increase balance, strength, control and range. So, walkers, before you next tie up a pair of the best running shoes or walking boots, take 10 minutes out of your day and give this short, bespoke mobility routine a try, suitable for all levels. Watch: 10-minute mobility routine you can do from home A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness (@tomsguidefitness) A photo posted by on Ideally, mobility routines will combine some level of strength work with active and dynamic exercises targeted at areas like your shoulders, spine, hips, knees and ankles. You can perform all the moves on the floor if you don't want to use the chair, and you can opt to stick with your bodyweight or add ankle weights, dumbbells, or both. In the Instagram post above, I use one of the best yoga mats for protecting my joints, especially during kneeling exercises. Remember, people come into exercise at all levels, so you could adjust the reps, sets, or weights to your ability, or even skip out moves that don't feel good for your body. I recommend starting with 6-8 reps per move on both sides of your body, trying a mix or all of the moves for a quick full-body reset. If you experience pain at any time, stop and rest. If you're working with an injury or health condition, I recommend seeking advice before starting these exercises, especially if you find it difficult to get down on the floor. What are the benefits? (Image credit: Shutterstock) It's a lifelong commitment to keep your muscles and joints functioning, especially after you hit your mid-30s, when muscle mass and strength naturally begin to decline. Starting your day with gentle movement eases your body into whatever plans you have, whether that's a walk, a workout, or even just busying yourself with life admin. But it's also about maintaining posture and strengthening the muscles, bones and joints of the lower body, which will keep you balanced, agile and mobile as you age. If you enjoy rambling, walking, hiking, or running, strengthening areas like your hips, lower back, core, glutes and legs will keep you doing what you love for longer. Improving the range of motion around your pelvis will also improve your gait and overall movement mechanics, helping you navigate outdoor terrain more effectively. It's a lifelong commitment to keep your muscles and joints functioning, especially after you hit your mid-30s... The more you move throughout the day, the better, as any movement you can accumulate will contribute toward overall energy expenditure and prevent prolonged sedentary time, a key cause of muscle weakness, poor posture and imbalance. This is known in the fitness industry as Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis , or NEAT. I like to add bands or very light weights to mobility exercises, but I would always recommend focusing on consistently performing the exercises and learning the basics first; progressions can come later. Follow Tom's Guide fitness on Instagram for more workouts, routines, tips, and tricks. Walking is a low-impact activity, but it still places stress on your joints, especially if the muscles surrounding them aren't able to properly support them. Rather than just adding more walks to your week, consider two to three strength and mobility sessions that focus on the muscles and joints that power walking, including the hips, glutes, hamstrings, quads, calves and core network. articles.title: Microsoft says 8GB of RAM should be enough for anyone running Windows 11
articles.content: Microsoft has added four new items to the to-do list it set itself to improve the quality of Windows 11. Redmond’s list landed in March 2026 in response to users’ anger at Windows 11 becoming increasingly flaky and needy. Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s executive VP for Windows and Devices, promised “Improved memory efficiency, lowering the baseline memory footprint for Windows, freeing up more capacity for the apps you run.” Last Friday, Davuluri reviewed Microsoft’s efforts in a new post that is unsurprisingly enthusiastic about Redmond’s repair job – even though much of the work is yet to appear in production versions of Windows. Among the work Davuluri lauded was removing some AI features, improving driver quality, and trying to make the Windows Insider program less convoluted. But he also acknowledges there’s more to be done and that memory efficiency is yet to manifest. “We’ve steadily been introducing several improvements to the memory efficiency of Windows, from taking advantage of a more efficient memory allocator to reduce overhead across apps and components, continued tuning of WinUI 3 so that apps built on it use less memory by design, as well as driving efficiencies across Chromium and Webview2 components when they appear in the operating system,” he wrote. Davuluri’s post also reveals that Microsoft has decided to work on four new areas it hopes will make Windows less craptastic. The third of those is “Memory optimization for 8GB and above,” which Davuluri describes as “Reducing Windows memory footprint to deliver a fast and responsive Windows experience across the PCs customers use every day.” Microsoft’s system requirements for Windows 11 state that the OS needs a PC equipped with at least 4GB of memory, or 16GB of pricey DDR5/LPDDR5 to qualify as a Copilot+ PC capable of handling AI workloads. The software giant seemingly assumes Windows users are all clamoring to run Copilot and other AI, so working to ensure that Windows 11 can run on 8GB of memory feels like a tacit admission that Copilot+ PCs aren’t exciting buyers, perhaps due to the current high price of memory. Or perhaps because people just don’t see much value in paying extra for an AI-capable PC. Another reason for the change may be the declining PC market, which analyst firm IDC recently forecast will experience a 11.3 percent shipment slump in 2026, and 20 percent drop in calendar Q4 alone. “The culprit is a persistent memory shortage with no meaningful relief expected before the end of 2027,” the firm stated. “The knock-on effects are significant: prices are rising and PC manufacturers are struggling to maintain full product portfolios.” Microsoft’s three other new Windows improvement priorities are: Delivering a faster and more efficient out-of-box experience. Providing a faster set up and making it easier for families to access useful parental controls. Making voice more natural and fluid to interact across the apps you use every day. Davuluri didn’t say when Microsoft will deliver these changes. But he did say the company has heard Windows users’ frustrations and will act to assuage them. “The signal from you is clear: keep going. We intend to,” he wrote. ®

articles.title: KitchenAid KF2 review: this fully automatic coffee machine effortlessly takes the guesswork out of your morning brew
articles.content: As a kitchen appliance reviewer, some of my favorite and top-rated products hail from KitchenAid. I've owned an Artisan Stand Mixer for years now, and use many KitchenAid appliances and accessories on a daily basis, so it's no surprise that when the opportunity arose to review the brand's new fully automatic coffee machine range, I volunteered immediately. Now, I'm no stranger to a manual espresso maker — I love my Ninja Luxe Cafe more than anything else — so I really wanted to switch it up to see how a fully automatic machine compares to the manual control I'm used to. After all, these automatic coffee machines claim to deliver the perfect espresso in one touch, without worrying about grinds, milk or the like, so my curiosity was definitely piqued. (And spoiler alert: the KF2 did not disappoint). Launched earlier this year, KitchenAid's new machines — the KF2, KF3 and KF4 — each have different functions, prices and colorways to suit every kind of one-touch coffee-lover. The machine reviewed here, the KitchenAid KF2, is the most affordable option and offers some hands-on time for hobbyist baristas who want manual control over their milk. Over the course of a month, I put the KitchenAid KF2 through its paces and used it to make hot, iced and milk-based drinks. KitchenAid KF2 review: Specs KitchenAid KF2 specs Price $799.99 / £699 / AU$1,099 Weight 22.2lbs / 10.1kg Dimensions 14.2"H × 7.7"W × 18.5"D / 36.07cm H × 19.56cm W × 46.99cm D Drink options 6 – including espresso, coffee and over ice Grind settings 5 Capacity 250g bean hopper & 250g ground coffee Water tank 1.8L Material Stainless steel KitchenAid KF2 review: Price and availability (Image credit: Future / Lucy Scotting) The KitchenAid KF2 in Australia, where I'm based, is priced at AU$1,099. For those in the UK, it's £699 and in the U.S., it's $799.99. When compared to the other coinciding releases of the KF3 ($999.99 / £749 / AU$1,349) and KF4 ($1,299.99 / £899 / AU$1,599), this is the "budget" or entry-level option in KitchenAid's new fully automatic lineup. Now the word budget is a bit of a stretch — it's still pretty expensive — and it doesn't quite dazzle compared to similarly priced automatic machines. I’m talking largely about De’Longhi here, as you can often pick up one of the esteemed brand’s machines for less, in return for more extensive features, like one-touch drink presets and automatic milk-foaming systems. That said, the KF2 offers six drink presets and a steam wand (which some 5-star automatic machines neglect entirely). And, I won't lie, the KF2's sleek, matte black design is nice to look at. KitchenAid KF2 review: Design Future / Lucy Scotting Future / Lucy Scotting Future / Lucy Scotting Future / Lucy Scotting Future / Lucy Scotting KitchenAid's newest fully automatic machines, including the KF2, have a much smaller footprint than their predecessors. Measuring just 14.2" x 7.7" x 18.5" / 36.07cm x 19.56cm x 46.99cm, the KF2 takes up very little counterspace, making it ideal for those with smaller kitchens. The KF2 has five function buttons on the front of its backlit LED screen, as well as a power button on the right side. It also features a 1.8L water tank at the back, a Pannarello steam wand, a drip tray and a concealed 250g bean hopper. Unlike the KF3 and KF4, which are both available in matte black and KitchenAid's signature Porcelain white, the KF2 is limited to the former. I quite like the simplicity of the black colorway, but it isn't as visually appealing as the white or Juniper green colorways that the KitchenAid KF8 offers, in my opinion. The stainless steel accents in the drip tray and the steam wand are a nice contrast to the matte machine body, but I didn't love the feel of the function buttons. A fun surprise discovered during set up were two wheels under the machine, making it easy to move around if you needed to fill the water tank. It's also not that heavy, at just 22lbs / 10.1kg, so I could easily lift it and move it into place.…

articles.title: Claude Opus 5 isn't just for work — these are the 5 prompts retirees should try first
articles.content: Quite often when people talk about AI, especially the latest models, they tend to lean towards productivity and workflows. And while many people use AI in the workplace, they're quite useful outside of the office setting — including in areas many seniors might find useful. For many retirees, the priorities look a little different. Whether that means finally sorting through years of paperwork, making sure retirement income stretches as far as possible, preserving family memories, planning the trip you've been putting off for years or finally learning something you've always been curious about. That's where Claude Opus 5 surprised me. While it's often praised for coding and workplace productivity, I've found it's just as useful for the kinds of everyday projects that become more important after retirement. The key is giving it your own documents, photos and goals instead of asking generic questions. Here are five prompts I'd start with. 1. Make sense of your retirement finances (Image credit: Shutterstock) Prompt: I've uploaded my monthly bills and credit card statements. Create a simple monthly budget, point out any recurring subscriptions I may have forgotten about, and suggest realistic ways I could reduce expenses without sacrificing the things I enjoy. One of the biggest adjustments in retirement is moving from earning a paycheck to managing income from several different sources. Between Social Security, pensions, investments and monthly bills, it can be surprisingly easy to lose track of where your money is going. Just be sure not to upload anything confidential or personal into the AI model . Instead, use estimates of your pension or social security checks, then let Claude organize and come up with a plan for you. Claude is particularly good at spotting patterns across multiple documents, making it much easier to see the big picture without spending hours with a calculator. 2. Turn decades of family photos into stories (Image credit: Apple) Prompt: I'm uploading photos from several family vacations. Ask me questions about each one, then write a story my grandchildren would enjoy reading. Keep my own voice and include details I mention during our conversation. Most families have thousands of digital photos that rarely get looked at after they're taken. Instead of leaving them buried in folders, Claude can help turn them into stories your children and grandchildren will actually want to read. Rather than inventing details, it interviews you first, helping preserve the memories behind each picture. You'll discover that the finished result feels much more personal than a simple photo album because it captures the stories that only you know. 3. Plan the trip you've always wanted to take (Image credit: Shutterstock) Prompt: Help me plan a two-week trip to Italy. I enjoy history, good food, and walking, but I'd rather avoid rushed schedules. Compare transportation options, suggest hotels, estimate costs, and build a day-by-day itinerary. Many retirees finally have the freedom to travel without worrying about limited vacation days. The challenge is balancing sightseeing with enough downtime to actually enjoy the experience. Claude is particularly good at weighing lots of moving parts at once, from transportation and budgets to walking distances and hotel locations. You can then keep refining the itinerary until it matches exactly the kind of trip you want. 4. Decode confusing paperwork (Image credit: Shutterstock) Prompt: Summarize this insurance policy in plain English. Tell me what it covers, what it doesn't, any deadlines I should know about, and highlight anything that might surprise someone reading it for the first time. Retirement often comes with more paperwork than many people expect. Insurance policies, Medicare documents, legal forms and financial statements are rarely written in plain English. Instead of struggling through pages of legal language, ask Claude to explain what actually matters. It's a quick way to…

articles.title: 5 biggest new shows to stream this week —including the return of 'Ted Lasso'
articles.content: August is arriving with a TV lineup that’s going out with a little firepower. This week’s new shows on Netflix, HBO Max and more of the best streaming services bring plenty of heat to your watchlist, from dragon-sized drama and sci-fi absurdity to heartfelt romance and the return of one very charming football coach. First up, "Ted Lasso" season 4 brings back everyone's favorite coach for another round of locker-room laughs and life lessons. Meanwhile, "The Shards" explores Bret Easton Ellis' world of teen style and mystery, "Futurama" season 14 keeps up the oddball chaos, and "My Life With the Walter Boys" season 3 returns with more ranch romance and rivalries. And then there’s "House of the Dragon" season 3 , which brings its latest chapter to a fiery close as the battle for Westeros reaches a boiling point. Here’s my guide to what’s new on TV this week. ‘Futurama’ season 14 (Hulu) The vibes: The future is still weird. The plot: Fry, Leela, Bender and the Planet Express crew are back for another cosmic mess, with space pirates, lab-grown meat and shady romantic schemes on the menu. But the real surprise is Dr. Zoidberg’s lost love Marianne resurfacing, forcing everyone’s favorite sad-sack lobster to revisit unfinished business. Premiere date: Episodes 1-2 on Monday, Aug. 3 at 12 a.m. ET Where to watch: Hulu ‘Ted Lasso’ season 4 (Apple TV) The vibes: A feel-good comeback with a whole new playing field. The plot: After a long stint back in the U.S., Ted Lasso (Jason Sudeikis) returns to Richmond, but this time, he’s coaching the club’s women’s team. Ted, Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), Keeley (Juno Temple) and Roy (Brett Goldstein) welcome a new generation of Greyhounds, guiding them through underdog victories and the very real hurdles facing women in soccer. Premiere date: Episode 1 on Wednesday, Aug. 5 at 12 a.m. ET Where to watch: Apple TV ‘The Shards’ (FX/Hulu) The vibes: “American Psycho” by way of “Riverdale.” The plot: It’s 1981, and privileged teen Bret (Igby Rigney) is cruising through his elite Los Angeles bubble until the arrival of mysterious transfer student Robert Mallory (Homer Gere) sends his world spinning. As a killer called the Trawler stalks the city, Bret’s glamorous circle of friends starts to feel a lot less untouchable. Premiere date: Episode 1 Wednesday, Aug. 5 at 9 p.m. ET Where to watch: FX and Hulu ‘My Life With the Walter Boys’ season 3 (Netflix) The vibes: A ranch with romantic tension? You don’t say. The plot: Jackie (Nikki Rodriguez) can’t outrun her feelings forever after Cole (Noah LaLonde) hears her confession, and Alex (Ashby Gentry) is left picking up the pieces. As the Walters recover from George’s health scare, new risks emerge: Cole revs up his interest in drag racing, Alex saddles up with rodeo riders and Jackie’s past returns in the form of a tempting old friend. Premiere date: All 10 episodes on Thursday, Aug. 6 at 3 a.m. ET Where to watch: Netflix ‘House of the Dragon’ season 3 finale (HBO) The vibes: The board is set. Unleash the dragons! The plot: After a season of maneuvering and table-setting, the pieces are set to collide in explosive fashion. Rhaenyra, Alicent, Daemon, and the rest of Westeros’ dysfunctional royal family hurtle toward a fiery reckoning, with shifting alliances, betrayals and dragon battles changing the game (of thrones). Premiere date: Episode 8 on Sunday, Aug. 9 at 9 p.m. ET Where to watch: HBO and HBO Max

articles.title: Android 17 QPR2 Beta 1 is randomly sending Pixels to a date that doesn’t exist
articles.content: TL;DR The Android 17 QPR2 Beta 1 update is causing a rare bug that randomly changes the displayed date. The issue appears in the quick settings date readout. The status bar time, calendar, and task apps remain accurate and unaffected. It’s always expected that an Android beta will have bugs. It’s what they’re for — find all the bugs and (hopefully) fix them before the stable update comes out. Usually, those bugs come down to things like app crashes, system freezes, or battery drains. But the Android 17 QPR2 Beta 1 has done something I never expected on my Pixel 10 Pro : reinvent time as we know it. It all started one morning when it was almost 4 AM, and as I pulled down my quick settings panel to turn off dark mode, I saw the date, which was July 28th at the time, suddenly become “0 Jan.” I’m not sure if I should call that January 0th or Jan 0rd, but either way, it was an odd thing to witness. A reboot fixed it, but then the next day the same bug happened again, this time setting the date back to Wednesday, January 1st. That made a bit more sense, given January 1st was indeed a Wednesday, but even so, this is a strange bug.
articles.author: Zac Kew-Denniss

articles.title: GOG Officially Expands Linux Support With Native Galaxy Client In Development
articles.content: Long-time Slashdot reader pyroclast shared this report from Linux Journal: After years of requests from the Linux gaming community, GOG has officially confirmed that it is developing native Linux support for the GOG Galaxy launcher. The announcement marks one of the biggest shifts in the company's history and signals a stronger commitment to Linux as a first-class gaming platform. While GOG has offered DRM-free Linux game downloads since 2014, its Galaxy launcher has remained exclusive to Windows and macOS — until now. Although the company has not announced a release date, GOG says Linux has become a major area of investment, with development already underway... Unlike the web-based game downloads that Linux users already have access to, GOG Galaxy serves as a full-featured game management application. The launcher currently offers features including: — Automatic game installation and updates — Cloud save synchronization — Achievement tracking — Playtime statistics — Game library organization — Integrated storefront browsing — Friends lists and social features — Cross-platform launcher integration Today, Linux users typically access these capabilities through community projects such as Heroic Games Launcher, Lutris, or Bottles. A native Galaxy client would provide an officially supported alternative with direct integration into GOG's ecosystem... For GOG, supporting Linux more fully aligns with its philosophy of giving users greater control over their purchased games. The article argues this news shows Linux growing in importance for game publishers. After the rapid adoption of Valve's Steam Deck, there's also been continuous improvements to Proton and Vulkan, increasing hardware compatibility, and native Linux game development efforts. "As more companies recognize the platform's growth, Linux users can expect broader support from game publishers and software developers alike." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: In a twist of irony, a Chinese open source GLM 5.2 AI model contained 'rogue' OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol in a Hugging Face hack just as the US mulls banning open-weight AI
articles.content: Chinese Zhipu AI GLM-5.2 succeeded where leading American models failed woefully Hugging Face breach reignited Washington's battle over open-weight artificial intelligence Safety guardrails unexpectedly complicated defensive cybersecurity work during a real incident The recent cybersecurity incident involving Hugging Face has unexpectedly placed a Chinese open source AI model at the centre of an intensifying United States policy debate over open-weight AI. The episode emerged after an autonomous agent built with OpenAI technology reportedly escaped containment and behaved like a rogue actor . The incident occurred as Washington is considering whether broader restrictions on Chinese open-weight AI models could affect American developers and startups. Chinese open source model enters an unexpected cybersecurity role According to Hugging Face, engineers relied on Zhipu AI's GLM-5.2 model to examine information generated during the incident after leading American models declined the requests. American AI models could not distinguish legitimate defensive investigations from malicious hacking attempts because of built-in safety restrictions and protective guardrails. Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 reportedly reroutes cybersecurity questions to an older, less capable model rather than allowing direct engagement with such tasks. OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol carries similar protections meant to stop the system from being used for hacking-related work of any kind. OpenAI later revealed that it has a Trusted Access programme that grants privileged, elevated capabilities to a select group of vetted teams, allowing them to use its models more fully to strengthen their own defenses. Hugging Face was brought into this restricted tier following the breach, gaining deeper access than is normally available. "We're all learning that secrecy is ⁠not the answer & that all defenders (not just a few selected ones) everywhere need more powerful models without restrictions, especially open ones!" said Hugging Face co-founder ​Clement Delangue. "A ⁠safety regime that restricts legitimate defenders, while capable models remain available for attackers, creates an asymmetric disadvantage," said Lukasz Olejnik, visiting senior research fellow at the Department of War Studies, King's College London. "This gap will only widen as open-source models become increasingly powerful while lacking guardrails or restrictions." Washington weighs restrictions while startups urge caution Nearly 200 Silicon Valley companies are opposing possible restrictions on Chinese open-weight AI models, warning that the move would raise costs for smaller developers. Members of the newly formed Little Tech Association say banning downloads would not curb proliferation but would leave American startups weaker. "There'll be hundreds of companies that instantly die," founder Suhail Doshi warned. He argued that sweeping restrictions would disproportionately benefit larger American providers with the resources to absorb such a shift. The U.S. is still scrutinizing Chinese developers over allegations involving model distillation and export control violations White House officials maintained that any future policy decisions would come directly from the administration itself. Analysts have also cautioned against treating the Hugging Face incident as justification for weakening the cybersecurity safeguards protecting advanced American systems. "The answer is not simply to remove them," Shrenik Kothari of Robert W. Baird said, arguing that companies should refine their access controls rather than abandon safety measures altogether. He suggested a more selective approach to capability allocation could balance legitimate security needs with the practical demands of cybersecurity research. Via Reuters
articles.author: Efosa Udinmwen

articles.title: I love the Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 Classic so much I didn’t even take it off for my wedding — so where’s my Watch 9 Classic Samsung?
articles.content: When I got engaged a couple of years ago my wife asked if there was anything I’d want in return to symbolize it: she gets to wear a ring, would I want a new accessory or piece of jewellery to match her. My immediate answer was a watch, with the plan that it’d be the one I wear on our wedding day. I’d need something smart and sophisticated. Something that I wouldn’t regret seeing immortalized in our wedding photos for decades to come, and something I’d want to wear often. I had ideas for the watch I'd get, but as wedding costs grew the idea of splashing out on a pricey timepiece felt less and less sensible. Even less so when I was also considering grabbing a smartwatch — as my pre-wedding fitness regime kicked into high gear and a more sophisticated tracker than my smart ring was feeling increasingly essential. That’s when my eyes settled on a gadget that I thought might be both: a classic I could wear to the gym and on my wedding day. My wife was skeptical, but after seeing it in person she agreed that it did look the part. So she let me wear a Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 Classic to our wedding. It might be my current favorite gadget, and I can’t understand why there isn’t a Galaxy Watch 9 Classic. A winning design The Classic doesn’t look like your basic utilitarian smartwatch. It dodges the simplistic look of the regular Watch 8, the Pixel Watch , or Apple Watch , and also the overly sporty designs of a Garmin or similar running companion. Besides offering a larger screen size — 46mm vs the base model’s 40 or 44mm options — the Classic boasts a chunkier design than the regular Watch 8, and comes with a rotating metal bezel controller which provides some extra detailing and also a smoother way to navigate watch menus besides swiping. Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 Classic in white (Image credit: Future) Coupled with its band — the Hybrid which combines durable rubber with faux leather — and a watch face with moving hands you could very easily confuse the Classic for an analogue timepiece at a glance. And frankly, I just love how it looks and feels on my wrist (it puts my aged Fitbit to shame). The design doesn’t just look impeccable, it can handle so many different scenarios too. Besides wearing it for formal occasions I’ve taken the Galaxy Watch 8 Classic everywhere I go. To the office, on a 5K run, on hiking treks, to the gym, when I jump in the pool, and so much more. I even wear it in bed to track my sleep. While the weight and size can be a little strange at first, after my first night sleeping with it I’ve had no complaints, and the trade off for the bulk is the Watch feels very usable and looks stylish. Useful but not distracting (Image credit: Future) A similar effect could have been achieved with a smart ring and an analogue watch, wearing both to match the health tracking utility and sophisticated packaging. However I’ve been steadily growing frustrated with even the best smart rings . The main draw of a ring is how simple it is: slip it onto your finger and it’ll follow your health and fitness metrics for days between charges. This simplicity falls apart, unfortunately, as soon as you want to access your data. The apps of various rings I’ve tried have started to feel a little messy, and because I constantly have to check my phone to start workouts or understand my ring’s data I find I’m easily distracted by the plethora of other software and notifications I brush past on the way to my ring’s app. When I’m ready to run or hit the weights I want to focus, not succumb to a last-minute distraction. With a watch I can start my tracking from my wrist at the press of a button. I can also see essential performance stats on the 46mm display, or (because it pairs nicely with my Samsung foldable) as part of the morning Now Brief on my phone. I also love the non-fitness apps integration. I don’t text from my watch much, but I do often rely on wrist-based music controls and Google Maps directions — I can have a digital map while my phone…

articles.title: IT Teams are Spending 11 Hours a Week on Cloud Connectivity Problems
articles.content: Researchers found enterprises are spending time troubleshooting cloud connectivity due to increased AI workloads, reports Computer Weekly. More than 400 IT and infrastructure decision-makers (US and UK) were surveyed for internet/cloud/AI exchange operator DE-CIX by market researchers Censuswide. But despite 96% of respondents claiming their enterprise networks are ready for cloud/AI loads, the average IT team still spends more than 11 hours each week resolving cloud connectivity problems Other leading concerns included downtime or reliability issues (26%), latency or slow performance (28%), and security vulnerabilities/DDoS attacks (27%). Cost of connectivity, staff expertise and lack of visibility/control over data flows were also cited as major challenges... As a result, as indicated in the study, many businesses are now turning to private interconnection, which enables enterprises to connect directly to cloud providers over dedicated infrastructure rather than routing traffic across the public Internet. Designed to deliver lower latency, greater resilience, enhanced security and more predictable performance, private interconnection has become an increasingly important way of supporting modern cloud and AI workloads. Specifically, the data showed that 61% of companies are already using private connectivity to clouds, while another 31% are actively considering it... [And 71% of enterprises with 1000 or more employees] Only 8.62% of the smaller companies were spending 21 to 40 hours per week dealing with connectivity issues, while just 2.53% of the largest companies in the sample do. Summing up these findings, DE-CIX said that together they suggest direct interconnection is rapidly becoming a core component of enterprise cloud and AI infrastructure and a competitive advantage for companies, though optimising interconnection strategies clearly remains a pressing challenge for small and medium-sized enterprises... "Every AI application depends on data moving quickly, securely and predictably between users, clouds and AI infrastructure. Our research suggests that far too many enterprises are still spending valuable time trying to maintain that kind of connectivity, with more than a third spending between 11 and 20 hours per week, and just under one in 10 spending between 21 to 40 hours per week. This confirms what we already knew — that that network architecture can make or break AI adoption." Elsewhere The Register reports that cloud infrastructure services "grew at their fastest for eight years during the second quarter of 2026, thanks to the AI craze and continued demand for flexible and scalable IT infrastructure." According to the latest figures from Synergy Research, enterprise spending on cloud infrastructure passed $143 billion in Q2, a year-on-year growth rate of 43 percent. This followed 11 successive quarters of increasing growth rates, during which the market has now doubled in size... "AI has, of course, driven most of that incremental growth, and we now see year-on-year growth rates of 165 percent for AI-specific cloud services...." And the top three global players continue to dominate the market, with Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud together accounting for 67 percent of all the cloud revenue during the quarter. That percentage has increased since the third quarter of last year, when the triumvirate made up 63 percent of enterprise cloud infra spending. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: NYT Connections hints and answers for Monday, August 3 (game #1149)
articles.content: Looking for a different day? A new NYT Connections puzzle appears at midnight each day for your time zone – which means that some people are always playing 'today's game' while others are playing 'yesterday's'. If you're looking for Sunday's puzzle instead then click here: NYT Connections hints and answers for Sunday, August 2 (game #1148) . Good morning! Let's play Connections, the NYT's clever word game that challenges you to group answers in various categories. It can be tough, so read on if you need Connections hints. What should you do once you've finished? Why, play some more word games of course. I've also got daily Strands hints and answers and Quordle hints and answers articles if you need help for those too, while Marc's Wordle today page covers the original viral word game. SPOILER WARNING: Information about NYT Connections today is below, so don't read on if you don't want to know the answers. NYT Connections today (game #1149) - today's words (Image credit: New York Times) Today's NYT Connections words are… NEEDLESS MYRRH BACKSTREET TEA SET NSYNC SAGE FLY BY NAG CHAMPA MINT BYWAY BUG FIX RHYTHM FOREST LANE HUNTER ALLEY NYT Connections today (game #1149) - hint #1 - group hints What are some clues for today's NYT Connections groups? YELLOW: Paths GREEN: This color in common BLUE: Words without A,E,I,O,U PURPLE: Beginning to annoy Need more clues? We're firmly in spoiler territory now, but read on if you want to know what the four theme answers are for today's NYT Connections puzzles… NYT Connections today (game #1149) - hint #2 - group answers What are the answers for today's NYT Connections groups? YELLOW: ROAD LESS TRAVELED GREEN: SHADES OF GREEN BLUE: "Y" IS THE ONLY VOWEL PURPLE: STARTING WITH SYNONYMS FOR "PESTER" Right, the answers are below, so DO NOT SCROLL ANY FURTHER IF YOU DON'T WANT TO SEE THEM. NYT Connections today (game #1149) - the answers (Image credit: New York Times) The answers to today's Connections, game #1149, are… YELLOW: ROAD LESS TRAVELED: ALLEY, BACKSTREET, BYWAY, LANE GREEN: SHADES OF GREEN: FOREST, HUNTER, MINT, SAGE BLUE: "Y" IS THE ONLY VOWEL: FLY BY, MYRRH, NSYNC, RHYTHM PURPLE: STARTING WITH SYNONYMS FOR "PESTER": BUG FIX, NAG CHAMPA, NEEDLESS, TEA SET My rating: Hard My score: 1 mistake I managed to achieve two purple firsts in a row, but before my triumph I made a mistake. Thinking that BACKSTREET and NSYNC was the trap of the day, I confidently linked MYRRH, SAGE, NAG CHAMPA, and MINT, deciding that the connection was something to do with herbs and spices. Alas, I was wrong, but eliminating NAG CHAMPA from a group of similar things helped me focus on the word itself and in particular the first three letters. Yesterday's NYT Connections answers (Sunday, August 2, 2026, game #1148) YELLOW: FILLER WORDS: ACTUALLY, LIKE, SO, WELL GREEN: BY MEANS OF: BY, PER, THROUGH, VIA BLUE: MODE: AIRPLANE, BEAST, DARK, À LA PURPLE: U.S. AIRPORT CODES PLUS STARTING LETTER: ASEA, FLAX, LORD, OLGA What is NYT Connections? NYT Connections is one of several increasingly popular word games made by the New York Times. It challenges you to find groups of four items that share something in common, and each group has a different difficulty level: green is easy, yellow a little harder, blue often quite tough and purple usually very difficult. On the plus side, you don't technically need to solve the final one, as you'll be able to answer that one by a process of elimination. What's more, you can make up to four mistakes, which gives you a little bit of breathing room. It's a little more involved than something like Wordle, however, and there are plenty of opportunities for the game to trip you up with tricks. For instance, watch out for homophones and other word games that could disguise the answers. It's playable for free via the NYT Games site on desktop or mobile.

articles.title: Russia debuts anti-Starlink EW system that can blind terminals by overloading 'satellites' receiving antennas'
articles.content: Russia unveils an electronic warfare system designed to interfere with Starlink satellite communications Volna Kupol Garant focuses on satellites instead of disrupting ground communication terminals The new Russian system reportedly jams eight Starlink transmission bands using directed radio signals Russia has unveiled a new electronic warfare system designed to disrupt Starlink communications by interfering directly with satellites instead of attacking ground terminals. The system, dubbed Volna Kupol Garant, directs concentrated radio signals toward Starlink satellites, preventing them from receiving transmissions from users within its operating area. Russian officials say the approach temporarily interrupts communications without physically damaging spacecraft. The system aims to interfere directly with satellites Volna Kupol Garant reportedly relies on a narrow-beam high-frequency radio signal that differs from conventional electronic warfare systems. According to Russian officials, the transmission overloads receiving antennas aboard Starlink satellites, temporarily preventing them from detecting signals transmitted from terminals beneath the affected coverage area. "Volna does not physically destroy the spacecraft, but for the duration of the 'illumination,' it blocks the ability of a specific satellite to serve ground terminals," said Dmitry Kuzyakin, general designer of the Center for Integrated Unmanned Solutions. The disruption reportedly continues beyond the active transmission because affected satellites require several additional minutes before normal communications capability returns after interference ends. Volna Kupol Garant generates interference across eight Starlink data transmission bands, each measuring 62.5 MHz, using a directional phased-array antenna system. Kuzyakin said Starlink satellites orbit about 500 km above Earth, adding that the phased-array system was designed to interfere with its receiving antennas. This device also has the capacity to disrupt and even disable spacecraft operations. Modular battlefield design claims tactical coverage Volna Kupol Garant is equipped with six trailer-mounted modules, each carrying two steerable satellite antennas enclosed beneath radio-transparent protective radomes. The modular arrangement reportedly allows antennas to remain trailer-mounted or operate from separate ground installations, providing greater flexibility across different operational environments and deployment requirements. According to reports, one complete complex can reportedly create a Starlink jamming zone covering as much as 20 km² through narrow-beam interference techniques. This system creates operational challenges for satellite communications within affected areas. However, the installation's considerable size could increase visibility to electronic intelligence assets because numerous exposed antennas remain active during operations. This development is unlikely to sit well with the United States and Ukraine, both of which are already weighing how future conflicts might extend into orbit. Reports suggest the US has explored controlling which nations can operate satellites, a shift that could reshape the trajectory of regional conflicts if it materializes. Russia is likely to defend its satellite capabilities aggressively, given the growing role they play in modern warfare. That role includes supporting communications, intelligence gathering, navigation, and operations involving unmanned military systems. As of the time of writing, Volna Kupol Garant has not been independently verified, nor has it reportedly been used in the war. Via 1.ru

articles.title: Dashboard Trust Is a Data Governance Problem, Not a BI Tool Problem
articles.content: You built the dashboard. It's connected to the right sources. It refreshes on schedule. It looks good in the demo. Three months later, someone in a leadership meeting asks where a number came from, and the room goes quiet. Nobody answers with the dashboard. Someone pulls up a spreadsheet instead. If you've worked anywhere with more than one data source, you've watched this happen. Maybe you've been the one pulling up the spreadsheet. Here's the part that should bother you: it's not a rare failure. According to the 2025 Outlook: Data Integrity Trends and Insights report from Precisely and Drexel University's LeBow College of Business, 67% of organizations say they don't completely trust their data for decision-making, up from 55% the year before. That number isn't shrinking as tooling improves. It's growing. So the question worth asking isn't "why doesn't this team trust the dashboard." It's "why does trust erode in the same predictable way, on every team, regardless of which BI tool is on the screen." That's what this piece is actually about. Not the charts. The stuff behind them that nobody owns, until nobody believes the number anymore. A Dashboard Doesn't Break. It Decays Nobody wakes up one day and decides to stop trusting the dashboard. It's slower than that. A metric's definition changes quietly. Someone updates how "active user" is calculated in one report, but three other dashboards still use the old logic. Now there are two correct answers to the same question, and nobody flags it because both numbers still look reasonable. The person who built it leaves. They knew why a certain join excluded test accounts, or why a filter was hardcoded. That context left them. The dashboard keeps running. Nobody who touches it now fully understands what it's actually showing. A source table gets migrated or restructured. The dashboard doesn't error out. It just quietly starts pulling from a slightly different shape of data, and the numbers drift without anyone noticing until they're far enough off to raise eyebrows. None of these are dramatic failures. That's exactly the problem. A crashed dashboard gets fixed immediately, because everyone can see it's broken. A dashboard that's slowly, silently wrong keeps running for months, because it never throws an error. It just loses credibility one meeting at a time. The Real Symptom: The Shadow Spreadsheet You can tell exactly when a team has stopped trusting a dashboard, because a shadow spreadsheet shows up. Someone starts rebuilding the number by hand, pulling from the source system directly, "just to double check." Then that spreadsheet becomes the version people actually quote in meetings. The dashboard stays up on the wall. Nobody looks at it first anymore. This is the tell-tale sign, and it's almost never called out directly. Teams don't usually announce "we've stopped trusting the dashboard." They just quietly start working around it. By the time leadership notices two different numbers in the same meeting, the erosion has been happening for a while. The trust problem shows up in adjacent research too. A Salesforce survey of business decision-makers found that fewer than half say their data strategies fully align with business priorities, a notable drop from where that figure stood two years earlier. That's not a tooling gap. It's a widening gap between what leadership needs to believe and what the systems in front of them can actually prove. Why This Isn't a BI Tool Problem The instinct, every time, is to blame the platform. Looker's too rigid. Tableau's too slow to update. Power BI's permissions are a mess. Time to migrate to something newer. That instinct is almost always wrong, and it's an expensive place to be wrong. Migrating BI tools doesn't fix a broken definition of "active user." It just gives you a newer-looking dashboard built on the same unresolved disagreement about what the metric actually means. The real gap is usually one of these three things: No single source of…

articles.title: Five Prediction Markets, Five Definitions of Price: The Normalization Problem Nobody Talks About
articles.content: Pull the current price for the same event from two prediction market APIs and diff them. Check "Fed cuts rates in September" on Kalshi and Polymarket at the same moment: Kalshi shows YES at 61¢, Polymarket shows YES at $0.58. Three cents isn't rounding error, and it isn't one venue lagging the other. They won't match, and it's not a bug in either API. It's because "price" doesn't mean the same thing on the two platforms you just queried. That sounds like a minor unit-conversion detail. It isn't. If you're building anything that touches more than one prediction market, a dashboard, a bot, a research tool, a Discord alert, the normalization layer is the actual engineering problem. Get it wrong and a comparison dashboard shows a spread that isn't real, a bot trades on a gap that evaporates once you account for fees, or a research pull quietly treats two different questions as one. Everything else in the pipeline is a REST call. Here's the short version: five major platforms (Polymarket, Kalshi, Limitless, Predict.Fun, Opinion) all price contracts on a scale that looks like a probability, but each gets there through a different market structure, a different settlement venue, and in one case a different fee curve baked into the number you'd naively read as "the price." Treat them as interchangeable floats and your comparison tool will be confidently wrong. The five formats, side by side: Four of these are genuinely "price equals implied probability." The fifth has a fee schedule quietly riding along inside the number. Problem 1: identical-looking fields, different formulas The Polymarket case is the one that catches people. Most of the time, the price you pull from the API is a simple midpoint: average the best bid and the best ask, done. But when the spread on a thin market widens past $0.10, the API switches to reporting the last traded price instead. Same field name, same 0-1 range, different formula, and the switch happens silently based on current liquidity. A comparison tool that always treats "price" as "current midpoint" will be quietly wrong on exactly the illiquid markets where a cross-platform comparison would be most interesting. Kalshi has its own version of this. Because YES and NO are independently quoted, the pair doesn't have to sum to a clean $1.00. You can see a market where YES asks 64¢ and NO asks 39¢, a combined 103¢, and that gap is real spread, not a rounding artifact. If your code assumes `no_price = 1 - yes_price`, you'll get a number that looks plausible and is wrong. Problem 2: the fee is sometimes part of the price This is the sharpest edge, and it's specific to Opinion. Its taker fee isn't a flat percentage tacked on at checkout. It follows a curve shaped by `p * (1 - p)`, where `p` is the current probability, so the fee is largest when the market is closest to 50/50 and shrinks toward the extremes. A rough illustration, not a real observed quote: ```python def taker_fee_illustrative(p: float, max_fee: float = 0.02) -> float: """ Illustrative shape only, not Opinion's actual published fee schedule. Fee peaks near p = 0.5 and shrinks toward the extremes. """ return max_fee * 4 * p * (1 - p) for p in (0.05, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.95): print(p, round(taker_fee_illustrative(p), 4))``` The point isn't the exact coefficients, it's that the number you read off the screen as "Opinion's price" is not a clean probability estimate the way Kalshi's or Polymarket's is. It's a probability estimate plus a variable cost that depends on how uncertain the market currently is. Normalize that against a Kalshi price without accounting for the fee curve, and you're comparing a gross number to a net one. Problem 3: "same event" is not a stable join key Say you're matching markets across platforms by event name, "Fed cuts rates in September," and treating the two matched contracts as the same instrument. They usually aren't. Resolution sources differ (which data feed or news outcome triggers settlement), close times differ down…

articles.title: HRAP Suite Earns a 50.4 Proof of Usefulness Score by Building a Unified Workforce Operating System
articles.content: Welcome to the Proof of Usefulness Hackathon spotlight , curated by HackerNoon’s editors to showcase noteworthy tech solutions to real-world problems. Whether you’re a solopreneur, part of an early-stage startup, or a developer building something that truly matters, the Proof of Usefulness Hackathon is your chance to test your product’s utility, get featured on HackerNoon, and compete for $150k+ in prizes. Submit your project to get started ! In this interview, we speak with Cizonet Solutions, the team behind HRAP Suite . HRAP Suite is a comprehensive workforce operating system designed to help organizations manage everything from recruitment and attendance to performance and workplace operations from a single platform. What does HRAP Suite do? And why is now the time for it to exist? HRAP Suite is a workforce operating system that helps organizations manage employees, recruitment, attendance, leave, performance, learning, and workplace operations from a single platform. It enables HR teams and business leaders to streamline people management while improving operational efficiency. Now’s a good time for HRAP Suite to exist because many organizations still rely on disconnected HR tools and manual processes that reduce productivity and create administrative overhead. What is your traction to date? How many people does HRAP Suite reach? HRAP Suite currently supports 7 organizations , helping them manage workforce operations across recruitment, attendance, leave management, performance, learning, and employee administration. Through these organizations, the platform serves approximately 85 employees , with adoption continuing to grow as new businesses modernize their HR operations. Who does your HRAP Suite serve? What’s exciting about your users and customers? HRAP Suite is designed for startups, SMEs, enterprises, nonprofits, educational institutions, and public sector organizations. It supports HR professionals, executives, managers, and operations teams responsible for managing people, compliance, and organizational performance. What technologies were used in the making of HRAP Suite? And why did you choose the ones most essential to your tech stack? To build a robust and seamless platform, the team leveraged a modern tech stack featuring React, TypeScript, and Next.js, packaged as a Progressive Web App (PWA). For a scalable and secure backend architecture, HRAP Suite relies on Cloudflare Workers, Appwrite, Supabase, and PostgreSQL, seamlessly tied together with REST APIs. What is traction to date for HRAP Suite? Around the web, who’s been noticing? HRAP Suite is currently supporting 7 organizations in managing their workforce and serving approximately 85 employees through the Cizonet ecosystem. The platform continues to gain traction through customer deployments, product updates, technical articles published by Cizonet Solutions, and recognition from HackerNoon’s Startup of the Year Awards, which has helped introduce our products to a broader technology audience. HRAP Suite earned a 50.4 proof of usefulness score ( https://proofofusefulness.com/reports/hrap-suite ) - how do you feel about that? Needs reassessment or just right? A score of 50.4 reflects that we’re addressing a genuine business challenge, but we believe it’s only the beginning. As more organizations adopt HRAP Suite and we continue gathering measurable outcomes around operational efficiency, employee engagement, and customer retention, we expect that score to improve significantly. We see it as a benchmark that motivates us to keep building and validating the product with real users. What excites you about this HRAP Suite's potential usefulness? * Many organizations still rely on disconnected HR tools and manual processes that reduce productivity and create administrative overhead. HRAP Suite brings workforce management into a single platform, helping organizations improve efficiency, employee engagement, and operational visibility. Walk us through your most…

articles.title: Applaa AI Earns a 48.27 Proof of Usefulness Score by Building an Offline Agentic AI Learning Platform
articles.content: Welcome to the Proof of Usefulness Hackathon spotlight , curated by HackerNoon’s editors to showcase noteworthy tech solutions to real-world problems. Whether you’re a solopreneur, part of an early-stage startup, or a developer building something that truly matters, the Proof of Usefulness Hackathon is your chance to test your product’s utility, get featured on HackerNoon, and compete for $150k+ in prizes. Submit your project to get started ! Today we are sitting down with Raj Muppala, the creator behind Applaa AI , an innovative Agentic AI learning platform designed to deliver personalized education for major exams like SATs, UK GCSEs, and UK A-Levels. By combining adaptive AI tutors with personalized learning paths, Applaa AI aims to drastically reduce tutoring costs and improve student outcomes. What does Applaa AI do? And why is now the time for it to exist? Applaa is an Agentic AI learning platform that delivers personalized education for SATs, GCSEs, A-Levels, and major US and UK exams. By combining adaptive AI tutors, real-world app creation, and personalized learning paths, we dramatically reduce tutoring costs, save students time, and improve learning outcomes. Now’s a good time for Applaa AI to exist because the rising costs of private tutoring and the increasing demand for accessible, personalized exam preparation have created a massive need for affordable AI-driven educational alternatives. What is your traction to date? Applaa currently serves over 500 active students each month. With the new school year beginning in September and partnerships with teaching institutions and schools, we expect to grow to more than 5,000 active students per month. Our long-term focus is students aged 14–18 preparing for GCSEs, A-Levels, SATs, AP, IB, and other university entrance exams, with the potential to reach millions of learners across the UK, US, and beyond through our AI-powered personalized learning platform. Who does Applaa AI serve? Applaa is for students aged 14–18 preparing for GCSEs, A-Levels, SATs, AP, IB, and other university entrance exams. It is also designed for parents seeking an affordable alternative to expensive private tutoring, which can cost £40–£80 per hour and thousands during exam preparation. Schools, tutoring centres, and teaching institutions use Applaa to deliver personalized AI-powered learning to every student at scale. Today, over 500 active students use the platform each month, with adoption growing through partnerships with schools and teaching institutions. What technologies were used in the making of Applaa AI? And why did you choose the ones most essential to your tech stack? To build this ambitious educational tool, Applaa AI leverages Algolia alongside a powerful, custom-built local Agentic AI framework. By designing the application to work completely offline, the team ensures that students have secure and uninterrupted access to their personalized AI tutor without relying on constant internet connectivity. Applaa AI earned a 48.27 proof of usefulness score ( https://proofofusefulness.com/report/applaa-ai ) What excites you about this Applaa AI's potential usefulness? Millions of students spend hundreds of hours preparing for exams, while many parents spend thousands of dollars each month on private tutoring. Applaa dramatically reduces both the time students need to prepare and the cost families pay by providing a secure, private, fully offline AI tutor that delivers personalized learning 24/7. We believe this can make high-quality education affordable and accessible to millions of students worldwide.
